notes.made: Ferry wrote it, and it came out of the same sessions as the rest of Avalon: Chertsey, Compass Point, then the Power Station with Bob Clearmountain, Rhett Davies producing. Ferry plays keyboards, with Manzanera on lead guitar, Neil Hubbard on second guitar, Alan Spenner on bass, Andy Newmark on drums, Jimmy Maelen on percussion and Fonzi Thornton on backing vocals.
notes.context: Released in March 1982 ahead of the album, it got to number 6, Roxy's last UK top ten. Ferry has said the west of Ireland, where he started writing, is where the album's dark melancholy came from. The sleeve is Rossetti's 1872 painting Veronica Veronese. In America it barely registered (103 on the pop chart) until Bill Murray mumbled it at a Tokyo karaoke bar in Lost in Translation in 2003.

listen_for.where: the last stretch, after Ferry stops singing
listen_for.note: His vocal ends with well over a minute and a half still to run, and the song turns into a synthesizer instrumental. A pop single that gives its last third to the band was unusual then and is the reason it drifts rather than ends.
Fonzi Thornton sings the backing parts, as he does on most of Avalon, and he is a big part of its soul-record polish.

leads_to.title: Alone in Kyoto
leads_to.why: It sits on the same Lost in Translation soundtrack as Bill Murray's 'More Than This' (his karaoke take is a hidden track at the end of the CD), and it is the French end of the same late-night drift.

notes.unverified: Desmond's Lost in Translation claim checks out. I left out any US Hot 100 position: the album article gives 103, and the song article only gives 58 on the rock chart.
